content: Viaspan, also referred to as University of Wisconsin solution (UW solution), was the first preservation solution specifically designed for use in organ transplantation. It was the first intracellular-like preservation medium developed. This solution was created by Folkert Belzer and James Southard in the late 1980s, initially for the preservation of the pancreas. Shortly after its development, Viaspan replaced the Euro-Collins solution as the preferred medium for cold storage of livers, kidneys, and pancreas. It has also been utilized for the preservation of hearts and other organs. Despite the emergence of other preservation solutions that may offer certain advantages, Viaspan is still widely regarded as the gold standard for organ preservation. The development of Viaspan was guided by several key principles. First, osmotic concentration was maintained using metabolically inert substances such as lactobionate and raffinose, rather than glucose. Second, hydroxyethyl starch (HES) was included in the formulation to prevent edema. Third, the solution incorporated substances to scavenge free radicals, along with steroids and insulin, to enhance its protective effects.
